content.text:
AMZN’s Feb. 3–6 move looks like a coherent AI-capex repricing rather than a random four-day drift: the stock fell each session, from $238.62 on Feb. 3 to $210.32 on Feb. 6, with the largest daily leg on Feb. 6 after earnings and the two internal rolling signals both pointing down (-6.68% for Feb. 3–5 and -9.73% for Feb. 4–6) [1]. The pre-earnings weakness was already visible on Feb. 5, when AMZN closed down 4.42% at $222.69 amid a broader tech/AI selloff and investor focus on AWS growth, AI capex, and guidance ahead of results [2]. The post-close earnings release then supplied the firm-specific catalyst: Amazon reported strong headline growth—Q4 net sales up 14% to $213.4 billion and AWS sales up 24%—but also said free cash flow fell to $11.2 billion from $38.2 billion, mainly due to higher property and equipment spending tied to AI, and guided to about $200 billion of 2026 capex [3].

That capex number appears to explain why the selloff intensified despite decent operating data. AP reported that shares fell 11% after hours as investors were spooked by plans to lift capex nearly 60% to $200 billion from $128 billion, above the roughly $147 billion Wall Street expected, while Q4 profit was slightly below estimates [4]. Reuters likewise framed the Feb. 6 slide as a 9% drop driven by concern that Big Tech AI spending was becoming too large and too capital-intensive; it quoted analysts saying the magnitude of Amazon’s spend was materially above consensus and that the margin for error was shrinking [5]. This aligns with the regression’s 77% firm-specific attribution: the main shock was not weak demand in retail or cloud, but a reset in expected free cash flow, returns on invested capital, and AWS/AI monetization risk.

The industry and macro pieces also mattered, but they look secondary and partly overlapping. XLY, the consumer-discretionary proxy, fell on Feb. 3, Feb. 4, and especially Feb. 5 before rebounding on Feb. 6, consistent with the model’s 16% industry contribution and with Amazon’s large influence inside discretionary/platform-retail baskets [6]. Broader risk appetite was also poor into the earnings print: on Feb. 5, Reuters reported the S&P 500 down 1.32% and Nasdaq down 1.68% as Alphabet’s AI capex plans and software-disruption fears pressured mega-cap technology, with Amazon slipping ahead of results [7]. However, the market backdrop was not uniformly negative on Feb. 6—the S&P 500 rose 2.0% and Nasdaq 2.2% that day—so the 8% market attribution is best read as early-window drag rather than the main explanation for the Feb. 6 break [8]. Evidence is therefore strongest for a firm-specific capex/free-cash-flow shock, with industry and macro forces amplifying the first half of the episode rather than fully explaining the peak rolling decline.
